title: Taming Rogue AI Agents with Observability-Driven Evaluation — Jim Bennett, Galileo
talk_summary: The talk argues agent systems need observability-driven evals at each step, using LLM judges on sampled traces and human calibration. It recommends evals from prompt engineering through CI/CD and production alerting, not just final pass/fail.

takeaways.what_they_do: Instrument each agent run at every LLM/tool/agent step and score step-level metrics, not just final success, so failures are localized.
takeaways.evidence_quote: I need to be able to do these evaluations at every single component. It's not just that binary did my agent work yes or no question.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use a stronger/expensive LLM as judge on a sample of production traces while main agents use the cheapest capable model.
takeaways.evidence_quote: use a better LLM to score than the LLM you use in your application

takeaways.what_they_do: Score both whether the task completed and whether each step advanced toward the goal, distinguishing unhelpful-but-progressing runs from successful ones.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Action completion is did it actually do the thing it was asked to do... Action advancement is did it move forward towards the end goal?

takeaways.what_they_do: Humans review eval scores and retune judge prompts continuously because LLM judges can be wrong.
takeaways.evidence_quote: your metrics will never be perfect out the box. You need this continuous level of training.

takeaways.technique: Evals in CI/CD and production alerts
takeaways.what_they_do: Run eval suites during prompt/model changes and CI/CD, then monitor production traces with alerting for rogue behavior.
takeaways.evidence_quote: keep those in your dev cycle and your CI/CD pipelines and then you want to observe these in production

takeaways.what_they_do: Run an LLM over unstructured trace/eval data to identify failure patterns and suggest prompt/system-message fixes, with human approval.
takeaways.evidence_quote: an AI will go against all the data and say, 'This metric is low. How can I make it better?'
